chunks: My father narrated to me, may God be pleased with him, who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Ja'far ibn Uthman, from Abu Basir, who said: I was with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

A man said to him: May God improve you, there are people in Kufa who say a statement which they attribute to you. He said: What is it? He said: They say: Faith is different from Islam. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: Yes. The man said: Describe it to me. He said: Whoever testifies that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and acknowledges what came from God, and establishes prayer, and gives alms, and fasts the month of Ramadan, and performs pilgrimage to the House, he is a Muslim. I said: And what is faith? He said: Whoever testifies that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and acknowledges what came from God, and establishes prayer, and gives alms, and fasts the month of Ramadan, and performs pilgrimage to the House, and does not meet God with a sin for which the Fire has been declared, he is a believer. I said: May I be your ransom, which of us has not met God with a sin for which the Fire has been declared? He said: It is not where you are going (i.e., not that we have no sins at all), rather it is that he does not meet God with a sin for which the Fire has been declared and he has not repented from it.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Islam and Iman in Shia theology according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq uses this narration to articulate the Shia doctrine of *al-Manzilah bayn al-Manzilatain* (the position between the two positions), distinguishing between the external submission of Islam and the internal, purified state of Iman. The scholar clarifies that while outward adherence defines a Muslim, true Iman requires the absence of unrepented major sins (*kaba'ir*) that incur Hellfire, a nuance central to Shia theological debates regarding the fate of sinners.
